doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Verifying who played on film soundtracks with Doc Severinsen
summary: He, Gio Washington-Wright and Jai Florada work with Doc Severinsen and Cathy Leach to verify soundtrack personnel, such as the bugle player in Gunga Din.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: That’s right. One of the other things, and I’d like to share this with you is there’s a wonderful, wonderful musician, incredibly talented arranger/composer, you probably know him. He teaches down in Dallas. His name is Giovanni or Gio Washington-Wright. And he’s done tons and tons of transcriptions. I mean he’s a genius when it comes to that and playing. But about two years ago Doc Severinsen and his lady friend Catherine Leach, Cathy Leach, Dr. Cathy Leach, came to me and said, “You know there’s a lot of misinformation out there as relates who played what on different film soundtracks.” Okay? So would you be interested in working with Doc and I on verifying some of this information and obliterating some of the hearsay and that which is not verified? What are you kidding? Do a book with Doc? So I engaged Gio, I engaged Jai Florada. Gio being a historian and very knowledgeable about soundtracks. He also has access through the union to the actual contracts. Okay? So we have started to work on this book which Cathy said to me it may eventually become like a long-form article on verifying who played what when and where, and who it really is. Okay? So we start the research, we start digging in, and I really got into this. Okay? Because I’m a soundtrack fan too. So we got into who played this on this soundtrack and whatever. And we even found out who played overdubbing for Sam Jaffe on “Gunga Din.”

The bugle call. The guy’s name was Charles Hamilton and the way I got that was I was watching some old YouTubes of “Gunga Din,” “Gunga Din,” “Gunga Din,” right? And this woman comes on and she says, “That was my uncle, Charles Hamilton. He was a member of the RKO Studio Orchestra.” So with Gio’s help and Jai’s help and Cathy’s

research we went back into a lot of these films, even going back to some silent films that had recorded soundtracks on them. Okay? And again, this was an enlightenment, seeing who played what on these recordings. So I’ll share something, and this is something I have somewhat of an issue with and it goes back to the idea of verification. I have actually shown the AF of M contract to other musicians and it says right there, “Here’s who is playing on this session.” Okay? They won’t believe it. They won’t believe it. So you know there’s some stubbornness or ignorance out there, but this idea of too much information, unverified information or in my case spoof information out there, okay, you know it can sabotage our history, our history, which is viable, the history of music, and in this case the history of trumpet in film you know. But that’s a long term project that we’re having a lot of fun with. And my daughter Amy as I said is a librarian so she’s able to get into, as a professional she knows about these databases and different things all around the world, and you can kind of access, legally, all kinds of information about films, recordings, record dates. So it’s really a lot of fun. It’s a labor of love.
